925.title: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)
925.hook: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)
925.tomorrow: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)
925.howItsDone: Readers of the Ramcharitmanas begin with its opening invocations, and the line about the whole world being full of Sita and Ram is often recited on its own with folded hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tulsidas bowed to Vani and Vinayaka at the door of the Ramcharitmanas, and said he wrote for the happiness of his own heart. What did you do just for the joy of it? Day nine hundred twenty-five.

Speeches at a wedding usually go the same way. Thank the parents. Thank the friends who flew in. Thank the cooks. Then, if the speaker is brave, a joke about the uncle who argues with everyone. Tulsidas, standing at the door of his great poem, does something like that, but stranger. He bows to his teacher. He bows to the saints. And then, with what sounds like a straight face, he turns and bows to the wicked. The people who wish others harm. He means it. And the reason he gives is today's lesson.
screen: `HE BOWS TO THE TEACHER.` → `HE BOWS TO THE SAINTS.` → `THEN HE BOWS TO THE WICKED.`

segments.voice: The opening of the Ramcharitmanas is a long series of bows, and it's worth walking through them in order. First the teacher. Then the saints, and here Tulsidas has a lovely picture. He calls the company of good people a pilgrimage that walks: like Prayag, which the poem calls the king of pilgrimage places, but moving about the world on its own feet. You don't have to travel to it. It comes down your street. Then he turns, and bows to the wicked, sincerely, he says. People who are glad at another's loss and sad at another's gain. Why bow to them? He doesn't pretend they're good. Part of it is a poet's humility: he asks even the hostile reader to be kind to the poem. But the deeper reason comes in a picture of the world. Tulsidas says the maker made this world a mixture, the living and the lifeless, good qualities and faults, all woven together. And the saint, he says, is like the swan in the old story, that can take the milk out of milk mixed with water, and leave the water behind. The world won't be sorted for you in advance. Good and bad come mixed, sometimes inside the same person. The work is to take the milk. And then the bow gets wider still. Tulsidas says that knowing the whole world to be full of Sita and Ram, he bows to it all with joined palms. That's where the series of bows has been heading. Not saints on one side and the wicked on the other, but a whole mixed world, every part of it, greeted with folded hands before the story even starts.
screen: `A PILGRIMAGE THAT WALKS.` · `A BOW TO THE WICKED.` · `THE SWAN TAKES THE MILK.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD FULL OF SITA AND RAM.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring your palms together in front of your chest, if that's comfortable, or just rest your hands. Bring to mind three people, one at a time. Someone who's good to you. Someone you hardly notice. And someone you find difficult. For each one, don't change your opinion. Just look for the milk in the mixture: one small good thing that's really there. Hold it for a breath, and let a quiet bow go toward each of them, even if it's only inside. If you pray, you can hold all three before God. The bell holds the time.
Tulsidas. The poet who, at the door of the Ramcharitmanas, bowed to the saints, to the wicked, and to the whole world as full of Sita and Ram.
Your line: the swan takes the milk. Today, with one difficult person, be the swan: find the milk in the mixture. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

screen: `DAY 925 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TULSIDAS (THE RAMCHARITMANAS OPENING AND THE HANUMAN CHALISA, VERSE BY VERSE).`

926.title: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)
926.hook: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)
926.howItsDone: Devotees of Hanuman recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often from memory, at home and in temples, and some make a point of saying it on Tuesdays and Saturdays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tulsidas bowed to the saints, to the wicked, and to the whole world as full of Sita and Ram, and the swan took the milk from the water. Where did you find the milk in the mixture? Day nine hundred twenty-six.

A truck driver in traffic, murmuring under his breath. A student outside an exam hall, lips moving. A grandmother on a Tuesday evening, a small book open on her lap that she doesn't need to read because she knows every word. They could all be saying the same thing: a hymn to Hanuman, short enough to say in a few minutes, steady enough to lean on. Tradition gives it to Tulsidas, and the hymn signs his name near its end. Today we walk into it, verse by verse, from the first line.
screen: `MURMURED IN TRAFFIC.` → `KNOWN BY HEART.` → `THE HANUMAN CHALISA.`

segments.voice: The Chalisa doesn't start with Hanuman. It starts with a mirror. The first couplet says, roughly: with the dust from my teacher's lotus feet I polish the mirror of my mind, and then I sing the pure fame of Ram. Before praising anyone, clean the glass, so what you see isn't smudged by you. The second couplet is even more honest. Knowing myself to be without understanding, it says, I remember Hanuman, son of the wind. Give me strength, wisdom and knowledge, and take away my troubles. That's the posture of the whole hymn. Not I am strong. I'm not wise enough, so I'm calling on the one who is. Then the verses proper begin: victory to Hanuman, ocean of knowledge and virtue. And they go on to praise him piece by piece. His strength. His speed. His leap across the sea. The way he brought the healing herb that revived Lakshman. But listen for the line that says what all that strength is for. Hanuman, in the Chalisa, is the guard at Ram's door. All that power, and it's used for service, near Ram, doing what's needed. And near the end, the poet steps forward and gives his own name. Tulsidas, the hymn says, is forever Hari's servant, and he asks the Lord to make a home in his heart. So the man who once crossed a flooded river for his wife ends up describing himself the way he describes Hanuman: a servant. The strength the hymn asks for is a servant's strength, a strength that stands at the door.
screen: `POLISH THE MIRROR OF THE MIND.` · `WITHOUT UNDERSTANDING, I REMEMBER.` · `THE GUARD AT RAM'S DOOR.` · then, large: `TULSIDAS, FOREVER HARI'S SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow. Start where the hymn starts: with a mirror. Picture your mind as a glass with the day's smudges on it, a worry, a grudge, a hurry. Don't scrub. Just breathe on it, and with each breath out, let one smudge soften. Then, if it feels honest, admit one thing you don't understand right now, in your life or in the world. And ask, quietly, for the strength to serve anyway. If you pray, you can turn that asking to God, or to Hanuman, in whatever words you already use. The bell holds the time.
Tulsidas. The poet of Ram, to whom tradition gives the Hanuman Chalisa, the hymn that cleans the mirror of the mind and ends by calling Tulsidas forever Hari's servant.
Your line: polish the mirror. Today, before you judge something, polish the mirror for one breath. Day nine hundred twenty-six.

927.title: Surdas
927.hook: a singer by the river stops singing about himself
927.howItsDone: Songs from the Sursagar are sung in Krishna temples and homes in north India, and in the Pushti Marg tradition founded by Vallabhacharya they are part of the daily service before Krishna's image.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Hanuman Chalisa opened by polishing the mirror of the mind, and ended with Tulsidas calling himself Hari's servant. Did you polish the mirror before judging something? Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

A singer sits near a river and sings about himself. How low he has fallen. How far he is from God. How little he deserves. The songs are lovely, and they are sad. That is how one old account remembers Surdas before his life turned. Tradition says he was blind, and that he lived beside the Yamuna, in the country of Braj, where Krishna grew up. One day a teacher named Vallabhacharya passes by and stops to listen. He hears the sad songs through to the end. Then he says one thing, and it changes what Surdas sings from then on.
screen: `A SINGER BY THE RIVER.` → `SONGS ABOUT HIS OWN FAILINGS.` → `A TEACHER STOPS TO LISTEN.`

segments.voice: The account comes from a book of stories about Vallabha's followers, told in Braj, the language of that country. In it, the teacher says, roughly: why whine like this? Sing about the Lord's play, his lila. And Surdas does. He turns from his own sorrow to a child's life in a cowherd village. The songs carried under his name are called the Sursagar, the ocean of Sur, and they are full of small household things: a cradle, a churn of yogurt, a mother calling her boy in to eat. Here's one. Little Krishna comes to Yashoda with a complaint. Mother, when will my braid grow? You keep telling me to drink my milk and it will get long and thick like my brother Balarama's. I've drunk and drunk, and it's still short. A tiny boy, comparing hair with his big brother, suspecting his mother of a trick. That's the whole song. And it is a song about God. That's the move Surdas makes. Bhakti has a name for this kind of love: vatsalya, the tenderness of a parent for a child. Instead of looking up at God from far below, the singer stands where Yashoda stands and looks down, at someone small enough to worry about. Notice what happened to the singer's own failings. Nobody told him they didn't matter. He was told to look somewhere else. His attention moved off his own smallness and onto a child's. Tradition says he kept singing in that voice, the voice of mothers and cowherd girls, for the rest of his life. Over the next two days we'll hear him twice more: a boy accused of stealing butter, and girls arguing with a messenger.
screen: `WHY WHINE? SING HIS PLAY.` · `THE SURSAGAR: THE OCEAN OF SUR.` · `MOTHER, WHEN WILL MY BRAID GROW?` · then, large: `LOOK DOWN, LIKE A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Notice, without arguing with it, whatever your mind likes to sing about you: what's wrong, what's late, what isn't enough. Let it play for a breath or two. Then turn your attention gently, the way the teacher turned Surdas. Bring to mind someone small, or someone in your care: a child, a parent, a friend, even an animal. Hold them the way Yashoda holds a boy with a short braid, with a little worry and a lot of fondness. Stay there. If you pray, you can let that tenderness be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Surdas. A singer of Braj who, tradition says, was blind, and who turned from his own sorrow to sing of a child named Krishna.
Your line: look down, like a mother. Today, when your mind starts its sad song about you, turn toward someone smaller and hum about them instead, even silently. Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

928.title: Surdas
928.hook: a small boy with butter on his face makes his case
928.howItsDone: Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo is sung as a bhajan in homes and temples, and around Krishna's birthday, Janmashtami, children sometimes act out the butter thief's story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Surdas turned from his own sorrow to a little boy asking when his braid would grow. Who did you turn toward? Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

The complaint comes from the neighbors. Butter is missing from their houses again. Pots are cracked. There are small handprints. So the accused is brought before his mother, and the song lets us see his face, which still has a shine of butter on it. He doesn't cry. He doesn't run. He opens his mouth and begins his defense. This is one of the songs carried under the name of Surdas, and it plays like a tiny courtroom: one small boy, no lawyer, and an argument he has clearly been working on.
screen: `THE NEIGHBORS COMPLAIN.` → `BUTTER ON HIS FACE.` → `THE DEFENSE BEGINS.`

segments.voice: It opens with the line the whole song hangs on. Maiya mori, main nahin makhan khayo. Mother, I didn't eat the butter. Then the case, point by point. First: at dawn you sent me off behind the cows, and I wandered the forest all day. When would I have had time? Second: look at these arms. I'm a child. How could I reach a pot hung up high? Third: the cowherd boys have it in for me. They smeared it on my face themselves. Then he changes tactics and gets hurt. Mother, you're too trusting, you believe whatever they say. Maybe you think I'm somebody else's child. And then the big finish: here, take back my stick and my blanket. I quit. You've made me dance enough. And the song ends: Surdas says, then Yashoda smiled, and pulled him close against her heart. Case closed. The butter never comes up again. Why would a devotional poet spend a whole song on a child's fib? Earlier this year we heard the Bhagavata tell how the butter thief stole. Surdas adds the defense, and gives the last word to a mother's smile. Her love doesn't wait for the verdict. It doesn't need him to be innocent. And notice whose name sits in the last line. The singer writes himself into the yard, standing there as a witness, watching Yashoda laugh. For a singer the tradition remembers as blind, it's a striking place to stand: the one who sees the moment the scolding turns into a hug.
screen: `MOTHER, I DIDN'T EAT THE BUTTER.` · `DAWN, SMALL ARMS, JEALOUS FRIENDS.` · `TAKE BACK MY STICK. I QUIT.` · then, large: `YASHODA SMILED AND PULLED HIM CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind someone who gets things wrong around you and argues their way out of it: a child, a coworker, a friend, maybe you. Hear the defense the way Yashoda hears it, every point lined up, a little dramatic. Then, instead of ruling on it, picture smiling and opening your arms. You don't have to agree with the argument. Just let the warmth arrive before the verdict, and rest there. If you pray, you can bring that person into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Surdas. The singer who let a small boy argue his case, and gave the last line to his mother's smile.
Your line: warmth before the verdict. Today, when someone hands you their case for why it wasn't their fault, let your warmth arrive before your verdict. Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

929.title: Surdas
929.hook: a learned messenger comes to teach the gopis, and a bee gets an earful
929.carry: our one mind went with Shyam
929.howItsDone: Bhramargit songs from the Sursagar are sung in Krishna devotion, and the meeting of Uddhava and the gopis is retold in kirtan, dance and Ras Lila performances in the Braj region.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Surdas let a boy with butter on his face argue his case, and gave the last line to Yashoda's smile. Where did your warmth beat your verdict? Day nine hundred twenty-nine.

Krishna has gone. He grew up, left for the city of Mathura, and didn't come back. In Braj, the cowherd girls, the gopis, are still waiting at the edge of the village. Then a chariot comes down the road, and it isn't him. It's his friend Uddhava, a learned man, carrying a message. Krishna is everywhere, he tells them. Stop grieving for a body. Close your eyes, practice yoga, meditate on the one without form. He has come to teach them. He has not come expecting to be taught.
screen: `KRISHNA HAS GONE TO THE CITY.` → `A CHARIOT, BUT NOT HIM.` → `UDDHAVA BRINGS A LESSON.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata tells this scene, and in it one of the gopis, deep in her sorrow, starts talking to a bee that has landed near her, scolding it as if it were Krishna's go-between. That little bee became a doorway. The gopis' bee songs are called the bhramargit, and in the Sursagar Surdas fills them with sharp, funny, grieving answers to Uddhava. Here is one. Udho, man na bhaye das bees. Uddhava, we don't have ten or twenty minds. We had one, and it went with Shyam. So who's left here to meditate on your formless one? It's an airtight answer. Uddhava's method needs a mind to sit still. Theirs is gone, walked off down the road to Mathura. In other songs they needle him: you've hauled a load of yoga to a village of milkmaids; take your goods back to the city, nobody here is buying. And between the jokes they keep asking the bee: does he remember us? Does he ever talk about the river, the cows? Two ways toward God meet in this yard: knowledge of the formless, and love for one with a face. Surdas lets the gopis win the argument. The Bhagavata, for its part, says Uddhava left wishing he could be a creeper or a bush in Braj, just to be touched by the dust of their feet. But the scene doesn't mock him. He came carrying the highest teaching he knew, and the tradition keeps both roads open, the path of knowing and the path of love. What Surdas adds is the sound of love from the inside: a heart that has given its whole mind away and has nothing left over to meditate with.
screen: `A GOPI SCOLDS A BEE.` · `WE DON'T HAVE TEN OR TWENTY MINDS.` · `OUR ONE MIND WENT WITH SHYAM.` · then, large: `UDDHAVA WISHES TO BE A CREEPER IN BRAJ.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Notice how many minds came with you: the one making lists, the one replaying a conversation, the one checking the time. Ten or twenty. Don't fight them. Just ask, quietly: where has my one mind gone today? To a person? A worry? A hope? Let the answer be honest. Then let your attention rest wherever it truly is, and stay there, the way the gopis stayed with Krishna. If you pray, you can turn that one mind toward God. The bell holds the time.
Surdas. The singer who gave the gopis the last word against a learned messenger: we had one mind, and it went with Shyam.
Your line: our one mind went with Shyam. Today, notice where your one mind wanders when you aren't steering it, and give that place a moment of real attention. Day nine hundred twenty-nine.

930.title: Mirabai's songs
930.hook: a cup of poison, and a woman who laughs as she drinks it
930.howItsDone: Mira bhajans are sung in homes, temples and concerts, and her life is retold in plays, films and devotional story sessions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Surdas and the bee songs: we had one mind, and it went with Shyam. Where did yours wander? Day nine hundred thirty.

A cup is carried into a woman's room. Inside it, the song says, is poison, sent by the Rana, the head of the royal family she married into. She knows exactly what it is. She drinks it, and she laughs. And the poison, the song says, turned to nectar. That woman is Mirabai, and the remarkable thing is who tells the story. Not a court record. Songs sung in her voice. Today begins three days with Mira's songs, and the first question is simple: who is this woman, singing about a cup of poison?
screen: `A CUP FROM THE RANA.` → `SHE DRINKS, AND LAUGHS.` → `WHO IS SINGING?`

segments.voice: What reaches us of Mira comes mostly through songs sung under her name and stories told about her, and tradition weaves the two together. Tradition says she was a Rajput princess who loved Krishna from girlhood. One story: a wandering holy man gave the child a small image of Krishna, and she wouldn't let it go. Another: watching a wedding procession, she asked her mother who her own bridegroom would be, and her mother, half joking, pointed to Krishna. Mira took her at her word. Married into the royal house of Mewar, she kept singing and dancing in the temple among wandering sadhus, and her husband's family took it as a disgrace. Then the songs tell of the attempts to stop her: the cup of poison, and a basket said to hold a snake that, when she opened it, was a garland. Through it all she sings to Krishna as Giridhar, the one who lifted the mountain, and calls him her husband, her beloved, the one she belongs to. Now the honest part. Other singers have sung in Mira's voice too, and some readers ask which songs go back to Mira herself. What reaches us is still a voice, and a clear one. Not a saint on a pedestal. A woman who knows the poison is poison, drinks it anyway, and laughs, because she has already decided whose she is.
screen: `SONGS AND STORIES, WOVEN TOGETHER.` · `A PRINCESS WHO CHOSE KRISHNA.` · `POISON, AND A SNAKE THAT WAS A GARLAND.` · then, large: `SHE HAS ALREADY DECIDED WHOSE SHE IS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind something that has been handed to you bitter lately: a hard conversation, a task you dread, a piece of news. Don't pretend it's sweet. Mira doesn't; she knows what's in the cup. Hold it honestly for a few breaths. Then let your jaw loosen and the corners of your mouth soften, not a forced grin, just room for lightness next to the bitter thing. Notice that both can sit in you at once. If you pray, you can hold the bitter thing inside your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Mirabai's songs. The songs sung in Mira's voice, of a princess who chose Krishna as her husband and kept singing when her family tried to stop her.
Your line: she drinks, and laughs. Today, when something bitter arrives, call it bitter, honestly, and then see whether you can meet it with a little lightness anyway. Day nine hundred thirty.

what it means: a woman who sang to Krishna as her husband, and kept singing through her family's anger.

931.title: Mirabai's songs
931.hook: mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else
931.howItsDone: Mere to Giridhar Gopal is sung as a bhajan in homes, temples and concerts, often in a simple call-and-response that lets anyone join the refrain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai's songs began with a cup of poison she knew was poison, drank anyway, and laughed. Did anything bitter meet a little lightness? Day nine hundred thirty-one.

Some songs argue. Some plead. This one simply states a fact, the way you'd give someone your address. Mere to Giridhar Gopal, doosro na koi. Mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else. It's one of the songs sung in Mira's voice, and it's short enough to carry in your pocket. Today we walk through it line by line. And since today closes a week, we'll finish by looking back at three singers who each found a way to belong.
screen: `SOME SONGS ARGUE.` → `THIS ONE STATES A FACT.` → `MINE IS GIRIDHAR GOPAL.`

segments.voice: Mine is Giridhar Gopal, the mountain-lifter, the cowherd, and no one else. The one who wears the peacock-feather crown, he is my husband. That word, husband, is the scandal and the point. Tradition says she was married to a prince. In the song, she says plainly that she belongs to someone else. Then she counts what it cost. Father, mother, brothers, relatives: she has let them go. Sitting among the holy ones, she says, I've lost lok laj, the world's sense of shame. What can anyone do to me now? And then an image that's hard to forget. With my tears, again and again, I watered the vine of love. Now it has spread, and it bears its fruit of joy. Notice the order. Her freedom comes out of belonging. Not: I belong to no one, so I'm free. The reverse: I belong so completely to one that the world's opinion has lost its grip. That's a logic of bhakti, folded into one song. Now look back at the week. Tulsidas gave us Hanuman's song, a servant whose strength comes from the one he serves. Surdas stood in Yashoda's yard and turned his sorrow toward a child, gave a butter-faced boy his defense, and gave the gopis their answer: our one mind went with Shyam. And Mira says: mine is Giridhar, and no one else. Three singers, one shape. Each belongs to someone, and the belonging sets the song free.
screen: `HE IS MY HUSBAND.` · `I'VE LOST THE WORLD'S SHAME.` · `TEARS WATERED THE VINE OF LOVE.` · then, large: `THREE SINGERS, ONE SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath come and go slowly, like water poured on a young vine. Then ask one plain question: whose am I? Not what do I do, or what have I achieved. Whose. It might be a person, a community, God, a promise you keep. Let the answer come in your own words, or let it stay without words. Then notice whether some opinion out there has a little less grip on you than it did a minute ago. If you pray, you can rest in the one you belong to. The bell holds the time.
Mirabai's songs. Mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else: belonging so complete that the world's shame lost its hold.
Your line: mine is Giridhar Gopal. Today, before a moment you're nervous about, ask inside, whose am I? and walk in as that. Day nine hundred thirty-one.

fork.reveal: in her songs she keeps going: what can anyone do to me now? the belonging comes first, and the freedom follows from it.

original.note: Sanskrit and Hindi, in Devanagari: the cowherd, a name of Krishna, as in mere to Giridhar Gopal.

trapdoor: what you thought: a romantic song.
what it means: a declaration of belonging that frees her from the world's opinion.
what a scholar hears: calling Krishna her husband turns bhakti into a marriage bond, and the line about lok laj names exactly what that cost a woman of her world.
